source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Continue observation until seizure activity reaches 30 minutes, because treatment before that point can interfere with spontaneous seizure termination.","B":"Begin first-line benzodiazepine therapy promptly, because the AES initial-treatment phase for ongoing convulsive seizure activity starts at about 5 minutes.","C":"Delay antiseizure treatment until the client returns to baseline, because medication is indicated only when repeated seizures occur after consciousness returns.","D":"Treat the event as a simple self-limited seizure and provide supportive care only, because continuous convulsions do not meet emergency criteria before 10 minutes."}}
source_row.rationale: At 6 minutes of continuous generalized convulsive activity, the seizure has entered the AES initial-treatment phase, when a benzodiazepine is recommended promptly. Option B follows that treatment algorithm. Option A waits until 30 minutes and delays effective treatment. Option C delays medication until recovery despite ongoing convulsions. Option D incorrectly treats persistent 6-minute convulsive activity as an event needing supportive care alone.
source_row.source_detail: American Epilepsy Society evidence-based convulsive status epilepticus treatment algorithm — stabilization phase 0–5 minutes; initial therapy phase 5–20 minutes; benzodiazepines are recommended initial therapy for ongoing generalized convulsive seizure activity. AES evidence-based convulsive-status guideline remains the listed foundational treatment guidance in 2026 while an updated status-epilepticus guideline is in development; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, medical emergencies and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client has continuous generalized convulsive seizure activity lasting 6 minutes. Which action is most consistent with current treatment guidance?
